source.title: Steering CLIP's vision transformer with sparse autoencoders
source.authors: Sonia Joseph; Praneet Suresh; E. Gol'dfarb; Lorenz Hufe; Yossi Gandelsman; Robert Graham; D. Bzdok; W. Samek; Blake Richards

record.file_problem: none; the full paper and supplementary material are present.
record.tranche_reason: It examines whether CLIP vision-model neurons are polysemantic using maximally activating images, a conceptual test of V1 with a different model and analysis.
record.gate_note: The paper explicitly characterizes base-model neurons as highly polysemantic based on maximally activating images. Its neuron-ablation results report downstream task accuracy, not a direct measure of how many unrelated inputs activate a neuron, so those results are not recorded as polysemanticity rows. The reported neuron-versus-SAE concept-coverage comparison measures steering coverage rather than polysemantic responses and is recorded under none.
record.test_reason: The paper is about training SAEs on CLIP-ViT-B-32 and steering them; polysemanticity is assumed as motivation (citing Toy Models of Superposition). The only bearing on V1 is a one-line qualitative caption saying selected base-net units' top images look polysemantic, used to illustrate the SAE method's advantage. There is no count, no description of which unrelated inputs co-activate a unit, and no stated selection protocol for the shown units beyond being picked by the method's own Fτ* rule. The 'base net' units also appear to be residual-stream dimensions, since the SAEs and the control ablations are on the residual stream, rather than MLP neurons. Its reported results concern its own method's steerability and disentanglement performance.
record.authors_conclusion: Mostly right, but it over-weights polysemanticity. The authors' stated conclusions are three. First, CLIP SAEs show vision-specific sparsity (higher L0 for spatial tokens than GPT-2 SAEs). Second, 10-15% of features in deeper layers are steerable, with SAE features giving about 10x the concept coverage of base neurons. Third, suppressing SAE features improves CelebA and Waterbirds disentanglement and achieves state of the art on typographic-attack defense. The 'polysemantic neurons' remark is a figure caption, not a conclusion.
record.recipe_differences: Uses maximally activating images to examine vision-model units, but studies CLIP-ViT-B-32 and SAE features rather than reproducing the original neuron analysis on InceptionV1.

fits_no_version.finding: At layer 11, steering base units reached about 1% of a 5000-word vocabulary (about 50 concepts) versus about 11% (about 550) for SAE features.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: SAE features on CLIP-ViT-B-32 give much broader steering concept coverage than base-model units.

fits_no_version.finding: Qualitative top-activating images of selected base residual-stream units look mixed, while SAE features show blondeness, land/water backgrounds and typography.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: SAE features on CLIP's residual stream look more task-attribute-specific than base units in selected examples.

record.peer_reviewed: Accepted to the CVPR 2025 Workshop on Mechanistic Interpretability for Vision (MIV)
record.problems: The polysemanticity finding is qualitative and based on selected maximally activating images; the paper does not quantify how prevalent polysemantic neurons are. The reported concept-coverage result measures steering rather than neuron response semantics.
record.rows_left_out: Downstream task-ablation accuracies from Tables 1 and 5–8 are omitted because they measure task performance after ablation, not polysemantic responses. Other SAE sparsity and steering results do not measure a claim version.

untested.parts: Any quantified or systematically selected test of whether vision-model neurons respond to unrelated inputs; no InceptionV1; no MLP-neuron analysis.
All; no language-model neuron analysis (GPT-2 appears only for SAE L0 comparison).
All; superposition is cited as motivation only.
All; Sec. 6.1 notes the steerability metric cannot separate polysemantic from specific SAE features, but this concerns SAE features, not neurons.

record.verdict_notes: Downgraded from the reader's 'tests/T2/supports V1' because the polysemanticity statement is an unquantified illustration on method-selected units, probably residual-stream dimensions. No verdict is given.

versions.untested_parts: Does not test InceptionV1 neuron 4e:55 or quantify the prevalence of polysemantic neurons across image classifiers.
Language models and MLP neurons in transformer language models.

rows.subject: CLIP-ViT-B-32
rows.operation_detail: Inspected maximally activating images for base-model neurons and SAE features.
rows.measure: Qualitative polysemanticity of base-model neurons from maximally activating images
rows.value: The authors describe base-model neurons as highly polysemantic; the SAE features shown instead capture task-relevant attributes.
rows.note: The paper gives this as a qualitative finding; it does not provide a neuron count or quantify the degree of polysemanticity.
rows.check: Purely illustrative claim (Fig. 2, Fig. 10; Sec. 7.1.2 'base model neurons are highly polysemantic'). The units were selected by the method's own spurious-attribute criterion. The paper does not say which unrelated inputs they respond to or how many units were inspected. The units appear to be residual-stream basis dimensions, not MLP neurons, so the figure cannot show whether neurons respond to several unrelated inputs as V1 describes.

rows.subject: CLIP-ViT-B-32
rows.operation_detail: Compared concept-space coverage under neuron-level and SAE-feature-level steering.
rows.note: This compares steering coverage, not the frequency of neurons responding to unrelated inputs.
rows.check: Steering concept coverage of the paper's own SAE method versus base units. This is a method-performance comparison, not a polysemanticity measure; it arguably should not be a row.

source_check.scope: Only the listed rows, labels and statements were checked; presence is not whole-study approval.
